title: At the feast of Dedication (John 10:22–42)
hookLine: in winter, at Hanukkah in Solomon's porch, they ask him plainly

cards: "And it was at Jerusalem the feast of the dedication, and it was winter." Two little facts, and they set a whole scene.
The feast of the dedication is Hanukkah, whose own story is told in First Maccabees, a book that Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include.
And it's winter, cold enough that Jesus is walking under cover, in the colonnade called Solomon's porch.
A crowd gathers close around him there, maybe blocking his way, and asks the question that has followed him for chapters.

teach.b: First, the feast. Long before Jesus, a Greek king named Antiochus the Fourth set up pagan worship in the temple in Jerusalem and tried to stamp out Jewish practice. A family called the Maccabees led a revolt.
When they took back the temple, they cleansed it and dedicated it again, with an eight-day celebration. Hanukkah means dedication.
The well-known story of a small jar of oil burning for eight days is told later, in the Talmud. Jews keep Hanukkah to this day, lighting lights in winter.
So here is Jesus, at the feast that remembers the temple made holy again.
The crowd says: "How long dost thou make us to doubt? If thou be the Christ, tell us plainly." His answer: I've told you, and the works I do tell you. My sheep hear my voice.

teach.h: NO MAN SHALL PLUCK THEM OUT.
teach.b: Then a promise: "And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand." Pluck is the King James word; some modern Bibles say snatch, like a wolf grabbing a lamb.
And no one can pluck them out of my Father's hand, either. "I and my Father are one." The crowd hears it as blasphemy and picks up stones again.
He escapes across the Jordan, to the place where John baptized at the very start, and there, John says, many believed.

teach.h: I AND MY FATHER ARE ONE.
teach.b: The story circles back to where it began.

how: Jews keep Hanukkah for eight nights each winter, lighting one more light each night; Christians read this passage as Jesus's plain claim of unity with the Father and a promise that his own are held safe.

games.q: it's winter in the temple at Hanukkah, and a crowd surrounds you: if you're the Christ, tell us plainly. what does Jesus answer?
o: "yes, I am the Christ, and here is my proof."
"I told you, and ye believed not."
games.why: he says he has told them, and his works bear witness. then: "I and my Father are one," and they take up stones.

practice: If there's a candle or lamp nearby, light it or switch it on; if not, picture one, and watch the light for a moment.
Think of someone going through a winter right now, grief, illness, loneliness, fear, and picture them held safe in hands that won't let go, and yourself too, if you're in a winter of your own.
If you pray, hold them in the promise that no one can snatch them away; if not, simply keep the light company.
